That day, after taking leave of the Grand Preceptor, he divided his fifteen thousand troops into three columns, departed the Eastern Capital, and marched toward Liangshan Marsh.

p.src: The story now divides into two. Meanwhile, Song Jiang and his generals attacked the walls of Beijing day after day but could not take the city. How would Li Cheng and Wen Da dare come out to meet them in battle? Suo Chao's arrow wound was grave and had not yet healed, so there was no one else to offer battle. Seeing that the city would not fall, Song Jiang grew troubled. He had been away from the mountain for a long time, yet victory and defeat remained undecided. That night he sat dejectedly in the central command tent, lit the lamps and candles, and took out the Heavenly Book of the Mysterious Maiden. While reading, he suddenly reflected that the city had long been besieged without any relief force appearing; Dai Zong had gone back but had not yet returned. Silently he fell into a distracted state, unable to sleep or eat, when suddenly a junior officer reported, “The strategist has come to see you.” Wu Yong entered the central command tent and said to Song Jiang, “Our army has maintained this siege for so long, yet why has no relief force appeared, and why will no one inside the city come out to fight? Some time ago, three horsemen galloped out of the city. They must have been men sent by Grand Secretary Liang to the capital to report the emergency. His father-in-law, Grand Preceptor Cai, is certain to dispatch troops with all haste, and there will surely be a capable general among them. Suppose they use the stratagem of besieging Wei to rescue Zhao, and instead of coming to relieve the danger here, attack our stronghold at Liangshan—what shall we do then? Elder Brother, you must give this due thought. Let us first order the soldiers to make ready, though we must not all withdraw yet.” While they were speaking, Dai Zong, the Magic Messenger, arrived and reported, “In the Eastern Capital, Grand Preceptor Cai has summoned Guan Sheng of Pudong Commandery, the Great Blade, a descendant of Lord Guan, and sent him racing toward Liangshan Marsh with a formidable army. The chieftains in the stronghold cannot agree on a course of action. They ask that Elder Brother and the strategist recall the army and return quickly to relieve the stronghold's peril.” Wu Yong said, “Even so, we must not hurry back. Tonight, send the infantry ahead first, and leave two bodies of troops to lie in ambush on either side of Flying Tiger Ravine. When those inside the city learn that we are withdrawing, they will certainly pursue us. Unless we do this, our own army will fall into disorder first.” Song Jiang said, “The strategist's words are entirely right.” He issued orders at once, assigning Hua Rong, the Lesser Li Guang, to take five hundred soldiers and lie in ambush to the left of Flying Tiger Ravine. Lin Chong, the Panther Head, was to take five hundred soldiers and lie in ambush to the right of Flying Tiger Ravine. Next, Huyan Zhuo of the Twin Clubs was ordered to lead twenty-five cavalrymen, taking Ling Zhen and the wind-and-fire cannon and other artillery, to a point some ten or more li from the city. As soon as the pursuing troops appeared, they were to fire the signal cannon, whereupon the two ambushing forces would attack the pursuers together. At the same time, orders went out for the vanguard to withdraw, trailing their standards, sounding no war drums, and dispersing like rain and drifting clouds. They were not to fight if they met enemy troops, but to retreat slowly. The infantry rose at midnight and departed in order. It was not until around the fourth watch of the following morning that the entire army had withdrawn.

p.src: From the walls, they saw Song Jiang's troops dragging banners in their hands and carrying swords and axes on their shoulders, surging away in confusion as they struck camp, plainly seeming to be returning to the mountain. After observing carefully, the men on the walls reported to Grand Secretary Liang, “Today the Liangshan Marsh army has withdrawn in full. They have all gone back.” When Grand Secretary Liang heard this, he immediately summoned Li Cheng and Wen Da to confer. Wen Da said, “I expect the relief army from the capital has gone to seize Liangshan Marsh. Those rogues fear losing their lair and are hastening back in panic. We can pursue and strike them while the advantage is ours; we are certain to capture Song Jiang.” Before he had finished speaking, a dispatch rider arrived outside the city bearing a written order from the Eastern Capital, arranging for their forces to join in attacking the bandits' lair. “If they withdraw, pursue them at once.” Grand Secretary Liang therefore ordered Li Cheng and Wen Da each to lead a body of troops and pursue Song Jiang's army by the eastern and western routes.

p.src: Meanwhile, Song Jiang was leading his troops back when he saw forces deployed from the city in pursuit, so he fled for all he was worth. He retreated all the way beyond Flying Tiger Ravine, when suddenly the cannon thundered together behind him. Li Cheng and Wen Da were startled and reined in their warhorses to look. Behind them they saw banners thrusting against one another and heard war drums beating wildly. Li Cheng and Wen Da urgently turned their army about. From the left charged Hua Rong, the Lesser Li Guang, and from the right Lin Chong, the Panther Head, each leading five thousand troops and attacking from both sides. Caught unprepared, they realized they had fallen into a cunning trap and hurriedly withdrew their troops. Ahead, Huyan Zhuo appeared with a cavalry force and launched a fierce attack, battering Li Cheng and Wen Da until their golden helmets sat awry and their armor hung in tatters. They retreated into the city, shut the gates, and would not come out. Song Jiang's forces then returned in orderly succession. They had soon drawn near Liangshan Marsh when they happened to encounter Xuan Zan, the Ugly Commandery Consort, blocking the road. Song Jiang halted his soldiers and made camp for the time being. In secret, he sent men by secluded paths to cross the water and climb the mountain with a report, arranging for the land and water forces to support each other from both sides.

p.src: Meanwhile, in the naval stockade, Zhang Heng, the Boatman, conferred with his younger brother Zhang Shun, the White Streak in the Waves: “Brother, since the two of us came to this stronghold, we have never distinguished ourselves. We can only watch others boast of their abilities and eloquence, and must endure their scorn. Now Guan Sheng, the Great Blade of Pudong, has divided his troops into three columns to attack our stockade. Why don't the two of us raid his camp first, capture Guan Sheng, and win this great merit? Then we can hold our heads high before our brothers.” Zhang Shun said, “Elder Brother, we command only a few naval troops. If no one comes to support us, we shall merely invite ridicule.” Zhang Heng said, “If you are so overcautious, when will you ever achieve anything? If you will not go, so be it. I shall go alone tonight.” Zhang Shun earnestly remonstrated, but Zhang Heng would not listen. That night Zhang Heng mustered more than fifty small boats, with only three to five men aboard each. All wore light battle gear, carried spears of bitter bamboo, and bore willow-leaf sabers. Taking advantage of the faint moonlight and the silence of the cold dew, they steered the small boats straight toward the dry-land route. It was then about the second watch. Now Guan Sheng was reading by lamplight in the central command tent when a scout posted along the approaches quietly reported, “In the reed-flower marsh there are some forty or fifty small boats. Every man carries a long spear, and they have all gone into the reeds to lie in ambush on both sides. I do not know their purpose, so I have come especially to report it.” Hearing this, Guan Sheng gave a faint, cold smile. He secretly passed down orders at once, telling the troops how each was to prepare. The three divisions received their orders and concealed themselves. Meanwhile, Zhang Heng led two or three hundred men, hiding their traces and moving stealthily through the reeds until they reached the edge of the camp. They pulled apart the chevaux-de-frise and made straight for the central command. They saw the lamps and candles shining brightly in the tent, where Guan Sheng sat twirling his long beard and reading a military treatise. Zhang Heng rejoiced inwardly, leveled his long spear, and charged into the tent. A gong sounded beside him, and the troops raised a shout like the heavens collapsing, the earth splitting, mountains toppling, and rivers overturning. Terrified, Zhang Heng trailed his spear behind him, wheeled around, and fled. Ambushing troops sprang up on every side. Poor Zhang Heng was masterful in the water, but how could he escape the net spread across level ground? Not one of the two or three hundred men escaped. All were bound and driven before the command tent. Guan Sheng looked at them and cursed with a laugh: “You wanton grass bandits! How dare you insult me!” He had Zhang Heng placed in a prison cart and all the others put under guard. “Once Song Jiang has been captured, they shall all be escorted to the capital together.”

p.src: Leaving aside how Guan Sheng captured Zhang Heng, let us tell instead of the three Ruan chieftains in the naval stockade. While they were discussing matters and preparing to send someone to Brother Song Jiang for orders, Zhang Shun arrived and reported, “My brother ignored my earnest warnings and went to raid Guan Sheng’s camp. He was unexpectedly captured and is now confined in a prison cart.” When Ruan Xiaoqi heard this, he cried out, “We brothers have sworn to live and die together and to aid one another in good fortune and ill. You are his own flesh-and-blood brother—how could you let him go alone and be captured? If you will not rescue him, we three brothers will go ourselves.” Zhang Shun said, “We have not received our brother’s command, so I dare not act rashly.” Ruan Xiaoqi said, “By the time the order arrives, your brother will have been hacked into eight pieces.” Ruan Xiao’er and Ruan Xiaowu both said, “He is right.” Zhang Shun could not prevail against the three of them and had no choice but to agree. In the fourth watch that night, they mustered all the chieftains of the greater and lesser naval stockades, each commanding more than a hundred boats, and together charged toward Guan Sheng’s camp. The soldiers on shore saw warships crowding the water like ants and drawing close to the bank, and hurriedly reported it to their commander. Guan Sheng laughed. “Ignorant bandit curs! They are hardly worth worrying about!” He immediately summoned his chief officer and whispered instructions in his ear. Now the three Ruans led the way with Zhang Shun behind them. Shouting their battle cries, they rushed into the camp, only to find spears and swords standing upright and banners still flying, but not a single man in sight. The three Ruans were badly startled and turned to flee. A gong sounded before the command tent, and cavalry and infantry surged from both sides in eight divisions, closing around them in layer upon layer like the jaws of a winnowing basket and the rings of a wicker hamper. Seeing that matters had gone awry, Zhang Shun plunged into the water first with a splash. The three Ruans fought for a path and fled. Just as they hurried to the water’s edge, the troops behind overtook them; grappling hooks descended together and lassos flew through the air. “Living King Yama” Ruan Xiaoqi was hooked, hauled down sideways, and dragged away captive. Ruan Xiao’er, Ruan Xiaowu, and Zhang Shun, however, were rescued after a desperate struggle by Tong Wei and Tong Meng, whom “River-Mingling Dragon” Li Jun had brought with him.

p.src: We will not dwell on how Ruan Xiaoqi was captured and confined in a barred prison cart. The naval forces reported back to Liangshan Marsh, and Liu Tang sent Zhang Shun by water straight to Song Jiang’s camp to carry the news. Song Jiang then consulted with Wu Yong on how they might drive Guan Sheng back. Wu Yong said, “Let us fight him tomorrow and see how victory and defeat fall.” Before he had finished speaking, war drums suddenly thundered in unison. It was “Ugly Prince Consort” Xuan Zan, leading the three armies straight toward the main stockade. Song Jiang led his men out to meet him. Seeing Xuan Zan rein in beneath the gate banner and issue a challenge, he called, “Which of our foremost warriors will ride out and seize this fellow first?” At once “Little Li Guang” Hua Rong spurred forward, spear in hand, and charged straight at Xuan Zan. Xuan Zan swung his saber and met him. Back and forth, high and low, they fought for ten bouts; then Hua Rong feigned an opening, wheeled his horse, and fled. Xuan Zan pursued. Hua Rong secured his steel spear in its carrying ring, drew his bow and took an arrow, then, sitting sideways in his carved saddle, lightly extended his ape-like arm, turned, and loosed a shaft. Xuan Zan heard the bowstring twang just as the arrow arrived. He raised his saber to parry, and with a ringing clang the shaft struck its broad face. Seeing that his first arrow had missed, Hua Rong took a second, judged the distance more closely, and shot at Xuan Zan’s chest. Xuan Zan ducked down beside his stirrup and evaded that arrow too. Realizing how formidable Hua Rong was with the bow, Xuan Zan dared pursue no farther. He abruptly reined about and galloped back to his own lines. When Hua Rong saw that he was no longer being pursued, he hastily wheeled his horse and chased after Xuan Zan; then he drew a third arrow, closed in until Xuan Zan’s back was within range, and shot once more. A clang rang out as the arrow struck squarely against the heart-guard mirror on his back. Xuan Zan hurriedly galloped into his lines and sent a man to report to Guan Sheng.

p.src: Descendant of a meritorious minister of Han, Great-grandson of a valiant general of the Three Kingdoms. His embroidered banner streams, stirring Heaven’s hosts; Golden armor and green robe set each other off. His Red Hare steed surges through violet clouds; His Green Dragon saber glitters cold as ice. A mighty hero born within Pudong Commandery: Guan Sheng of the Great Saber, brave and righteous.

p.src: Seeing Guan Sheng’s extraordinary bearing, Song Jiang and Wu Yong secretly applauded him. Turning to their many valiant commanders, Song Jiang said, “The general is a true hero—his fame is well deserved!” Before he had finished, Lin Chong said angrily, “Since we brothers came to Liangshan Marsh, we have fought scores of battles great and small without once having our spirit broken. Why does our strategist belittle our own might?” With that, he leveled his spear, rode forth, and charged straight at Guan Sheng. When Guan Sheng saw him, he shouted, “You bandits of the marsh—how dare you turn your backs on the imperial court! I demand that Song Jiang alone fight me.” From beneath the gate banner Song Jiang called Lin Chong back, then spurred his own horse into the field. Bowing slightly to Guan Sheng, he saluted and said, “Song Jiang, a petty clerk of Yuncheng, respectfully presents himself and awaits the general’s judgment.” Guan Sheng said, “You were but a petty clerk. How dare you rebel against the imperial court?” Song Jiang replied, “It is because the imperial court lacks discernment and allows treacherous ministers to rule, while slanderers and sycophants monopolize power, appoint corrupt and oppressive officials, and bring ruin upon the common people under heaven. Song Jiang and his companions merely carry out Heaven’s justice and harbor no disloyal intent.” Guan Sheng roared, “Even with the imperial army before you, you persist in resisting! With your glib words and ingratiating looks, how dare you try to deceive me? Unless you dismount and surrender, I shall grind your bones and smash your body to pieces!” When “Thunderbolt” Qin Ming heard this, he flew into a rage. Brandishing his wolf-toothed mace, he spurred his mount and charged straight forward. Guan Sheng likewise spurred out to meet him and engaged Qin Ming. Afraid Qin Ming would claim the first merit, Lin Chong suddenly dashed forward and made straight for Guan Sheng. Amid the dusty haze of battle, the three horsemen whirled and fought like a revolving lantern. Watching them, Song Jiang feared that Guan Sheng might be injured and ordered the gong sounded to withdraw the troops. Lin Chong and Qin Ming rode back before their lines and said, “We were just about to seize that fellow. Why did you call off the battle, elder brother?” Song Jiang said, “Worthy brothers, we hold fast to loyalty and righteousness. It is not our wish to use strength to bully the weak. Even if we captured him on the battlefield, he would not submit, and we would only invite ridicule. I see that Guan Sheng is a brave and valiant general, born to a line of loyal ministers, with an ancestor revered as a god. If we could bring such a man up the mountain, I, Song Jiang, would gladly yield my place to him.” Neither Lin Chong nor Qin Ming was pleased. That day, both sides withdrew their forces.

u.src: Seeing Guan Sheng’s extraordinary bearing, Song Jiang and Wu Yong secretly applauded him. Turning to their many valiant commanders, Song Jiang said, “The general is a true hero—his fame is well deserved!”

Before he had finished, Lin Chong said angrily, “Since we brothers came to Liangshan Marsh, we have fought scores of battles great and small without once having our spirit broken. Why does our strategist belittle our own might?”
With that, he leveled his spear, rode forth, and charged straight at Guan Sheng.
When Guan Sheng saw him, he shouted, “You bandits of the marsh—how dare you turn your backs on the imperial court!
I demand that Song Jiang alone fight me.”

From beneath the gate banner Song Jiang called Lin Chong back, then spurred his own horse into the field. Bowing slightly to Guan Sheng, he saluted and said, “Song Jiang, a petty clerk of Yuncheng, respectfully presents himself and awaits the general’s judgment.”
Guan Sheng said, “You were but a petty clerk. How dare you rebel against the imperial court?”

Song Jiang replied, “It is because the imperial court lacks discernment and allows treacherous ministers to rule, while slanderers and sycophants monopolize power, appoint corrupt and oppressive officials, and bring ruin upon the common people under heaven.
Song Jiang and his companions merely carry out Heaven’s justice and harbor no disloyal intent.”
Guan Sheng roared, “Even with the imperial army before you, you persist in resisting! With your glib words and ingratiating looks, how dare you try to deceive me?
Unless you dismount and surrender, I shall grind your bones and smash your body to pieces!”
When “Thunderbolt” Qin Ming heard this, he flew into a rage. Brandishing his wolf-toothed mace, he spurred his mount and charged straight forward.
Guan Sheng likewise spurred out to meet him and engaged Qin Ming.
Afraid Qin Ming would claim the first merit, Lin Chong suddenly dashed forward and made straight for Guan Sheng.
Amid the dusty haze of battle, the three horsemen whirled and fought like a revolving lantern.
Watching them, Song Jiang feared that Guan Sheng might be injured and ordered the gong sounded to withdraw the troops.
Lin Chong and Qin Ming rode back before their lines and said, “We were just about to seize that fellow. Why did you call off the battle, elder brother?”
Song Jiang said, “Worthy brothers, we hold fast to loyalty and righteousness. It is not our wish to use strength to bully the weak.
Even if we captured him on the battlefield, he would not submit, and we would only invite ridicule.

I see that Guan Sheng is a brave and valiant general, born to a line of loyal ministers, with an ancestor revered as a god. If we could bring such a man up the mountain, I, Song Jiang, would gladly yield my place to him.”
Neither Lin Chong nor Qin Ming was pleased.
That day, both sides withdrew their forces.

p.src: Now Guan Sheng returned to his camp, dismounted, and removed his armor. Privately he pondered, “I could not withstand those two generals together and was on the verge of losing to them, yet Song Jiang withdrew his troops. I cannot fathom what he intended.” He then ordered the soldiers to bring Zhang Heng and Ruan Xiaoqi from their barred carts and asked them, “Song Jiang is merely a petty clerk from Yuncheng. Why do you fellows submit to him?” Ruan Xiaoqi replied, “Our brother is renowned throughout Shandong and Hebei, and everyone calls him Song Gongming, the ‘Timely Rain’ and ‘Protector of Righteousness.’ How could an ignorant fellow like you, who knows neither propriety nor righteousness, ever understand?” Guan Sheng lowered his head and said nothing, then ordered them returned to their barred carts.

p.src: That night, troubled and unable to rest in the stronghold, Guan Sheng left the central command tent to look about. Moonlight filled the sky and frost gleamed across the ground, and he sighed without cease. A scout came forward and reported, “A bearded general has come alone on horseback, carrying a single whip, and asks to see the commander.” Guan Sheng said, “Did you not ask who he was?” The scout replied, “He carries neither armor nor weapon and refuses to give his name. He says only that he must see the commander.” Guan Sheng said, “If that is so, summon him here.” Before long, the man entered the tent and bowed before Guan Sheng. Guan Sheng thought his face somewhat familiar. Looking at him in the lamplight, he began to recognize him and asked who he was. The man said, “I beg you to dismiss the attendants.” Guan Sheng said, “There is no need.” The man said, “I am the junior general Huyan Zhuo. Formerly I commanded the imperial army’s chain-linked cavalry in a campaign against Liangshan Marsh. But I fell into the bandits’ treacherous scheme, lost the campaign, and could not return home. When I heard that you had arrived, General, my joy was beyond measure. This morning, when Lin Chong and Qin Ming were about to capture you on the battlefield, Song Jiang urgently recalled his troops, truly fearing that you might be harmed. He has long intended to submit to the court, but the other bandits refuse to follow him. He has secretly conferred with me, intending to induce them all to submit. If you will agree, tomorrow night take a light bow and short arrows, mount a swift horse, and enter the bandits’ stronghold directly by a side path. We shall capture Lin Chong and the other outlaws alive, escort them to the capital, and win merit together.” Guan Sheng was overjoyed when he had heard him out. He invited him farther into the tent and had wine set out for him. Huyan Zhuo explained in detail that Song Jiang held loyalty and righteousness above all else and had been forced by misfortune to join the bandits despite his innocence. The two men revealed their innermost thoughts to each other and harbored no further suspicion.

p.src: The next day, Song Jiang led out all his men and challenged the enemy to battle. Guan Sheng consulted Huyan Zhuo: “Today we should first defeat one of their leading warriors; then tonight we can carry out our plan.” Now Huyan Zhuo borrowed a spare suit of armor and put it on. He and Guan Sheng each mounted his horse and rode to the battlefront. From his formation Song Jiang loudly cursed Huyan Zhuo: “The stronghold never wronged you in the least. Why did you slip away secretly at night?” Huyan Zhuo retorted, “What great enterprise could scoundrels like you ever accomplish?” Song Jiang promptly ordered Huang Xin, the “Guardian of the Three Mountains,” to ride out. Brandishing his Sword of Mourning and urging on his mount, Huang Xin charged straight at Huyan Zhuo. The two horses met, and before they had fought ten bouts, Huyan Zhuo raised his whip and struck Huang Xin from the saddle. Soldiers rushed out from Song Jiang’s ranks, lifted Huang Xin, and carried him back. Guan Sheng was delighted and ordered the whole army, officers and men alike, to charge together. Huyan Zhuo said, “We must not pursue them. That fellow Wu Yong is full of marvelous stratagems. If we chase and attack, I fear the bandits may have laid a scheme.” Guan Sheng heeded him and urgently recalled his troops, and they all returned to their camp. Back in the central command tent, he set out wine for Huyan Zhuo and asked about Huang Xin, the “Guardian of the Three Mountains.” Huyan Zhuo said, “That man was originally an imperial official, the military superintendent of Qingzhou, but he joined Qin Ming and Hua Rong in becoming an outlaw. By striking down this bandit first today, we have blunted their arrogance. Our raid on their camp tonight is certain to succeed.” Guan Sheng was overjoyed. He issued orders for Xuan Zan and Hao Siwen to provide support by two routes, while he himself led five hundred cavalrymen equipped with light bows and short arrows and had Huyan Zhuo guide the way. They were to set out during the second watch, charge straight into Song Jiang’s camp around the third watch, and, at the signal of a cannon shot, attack from within and without in one concerted advance.

p.src: That night the moon shone as brightly as day. At dusk they finished arming themselves. The bells were removed from the horses, the men wore light armor, and the soldiers hurried silently with gags between their teeth. They all mounted, with Huyan Zhuo leading and the others following. After rounding a mountain path and traveling for about half a watch, they encountered thirty or fifty scouts ahead, who asked in low voices, “Is that not General Hu who comes? Song Gongming sent us here to welcome you.” Huyan Zhuo shouted, “Say nothing! Follow behind my horse!” Huyan Zhuo spurred ahead, with Guan Sheng riding behind him. After rounding another spur of the mountain, Huyan Zhuo pointed with the tip of his spear, and far away they saw a bowl-shaped red lantern. Guan Sheng reined in his horse and asked, “What is the place where that red lantern shines?” Huyan Zhuo said, “That is Song Gongming’s central command.” They hurried the men and horses onward. As they neared the red lantern, a cannon suddenly boomed, and all the soldiers followed close behind Guan Sheng and charged forward. But when they reached the red lantern and looked about, not a soul was there. Guan Sheng called for Huyan Zhuo, only to find that he too had vanished. Guan Sheng was horrified and realized he had fallen into a trap. As he hastily wheeled his horse around, drums and gongs sounded together from the surrounding hills. In their panic they fled without choosing a path, each soldier seeking only to save his own life. By the time Guan Sheng had turned his horse, only a few cavalrymen remained with him. As he rounded the mountain spur, another cannon boomed behind him beside the woods. Hooked poles sprang out from every side, dragging Guan Sheng from his carved saddle. His sword and horse were seized, his armor stripped away, and, shoved from before and behind, he was taken to the main stronghold.

p.src: At once Xuan Zan spurred forward and shouted abuse: “Wretched bandits! Whoever stands against me dies; whoever gets out of my way lives!” Qin Ming flew into a rage, urged his horse on, and swung his wolf-toothed mace straight at Xuan Zan. Their horses met, and they fought for several bouts. When Sun Li turned toward them, Xuan Zan panicked and his swordplay lost all proper form; Qin Ming struck him with his mace and knocked him from his horse. The whole army raised a shout, rushed forward, and seized him. Meanwhile Li Ying, the Sky-Swooping Eagle, led troops great and small in a charge into Guan Sheng’s camp. First he rescued Zhang Heng, Ruan Xiaoqi, and the captured sailors; then he seized all the provisions and horses and went on to enlist the scattered remnants of the defeated force. Song Jiang assembled the company and returned to the mountain; by then the eastern sky was beginning to brighten. They took their places in the Hall of Loyalty and Righteousness, and before long Guan Sheng, Xuan Zan, and Hao Siwen were brought in separately under guard. At the sight of them, Song Jiang hurried down from the hall, ordered the soldiers back, and personally untied their bonds. He helped Guan Sheng into the central chair, then bowed his head to the floor before him, kowtowing and confessing his offense: “We are desperate fugitives who have affronted your tigerish might. I beg you to forgive us.” Guan Sheng hastily returned the courtesy, but remained speechless, not knowing what to do with himself. Huyan Zhuo also stepped forward and pleaded guilty: “Once I had received your orders, I dared not disobey. I earnestly beg the general to pardon my offense in deceiving you.” Seeing how deeply all the chiefs valued honor and fellowship, Guan Sheng turned to Xuan Zan and Hao Siwen and asked, “Now that we have been captured and brought here, what shall we do?” The two replied, “We shall obey your command in all things.” Guan Sheng said, “We have no face to return to the capital. The three of us ask only that you grant us a swift death!” Song Jiang said, “Why do you speak so? General, if you do not disdain our humble company, join us in carrying out Heaven’s justice. If you are unwilling, we dare not detain you against your will; we shall send you back to the capital this very day.” Guan Sheng replied, “Men call you Song Gongming the Loyal and Righteous, and the name is no empty praise. Today we have no home to return to and no country that will receive us. We wish to serve beneath your banner as common soldiers.” Song Jiang was overjoyed. That day, while a banquet was held in celebration, men were sent to summon the fleeing defeated soldiers to surrender, and another five to seven thousand men and horses were gained. The old and the young among the troops were immediately given silver and released to return home. Meanwhile Xue Yong was dispatched with a letter to Pudong to bring Guan Sheng’s family, but there is no need to dwell on that.

I have a plan. Let this night pass. Tomorrow we shall raise our forces again and attack Beijing; we are certain to succeed.” Guan Sheng rose and said, “I have no other way to repay you for sparing my life. p.src: Now Counselor Liang was drinking in the city with Suo Chao, who had just recovered from his wounds, when a scout came to report: “Guan Sheng, Xuan Zan, Hao Siwen, and all their troops have been captured by Song Jiang and have already joined his band. The forces of Liangshan Marsh have now arrived again.” When Counselor Liang heard this, he was so terrified that he stared blankly, utterly at a loss. Then Suo Chao declared, “Last time I was struck by the bandits’ treacherous arrow. This time I shall avenge that injury.” Counselor Liang immediately rewarded Suo Chao and ordered him to lead his own troops out of the city to meet the enemy. Li Cheng and Wen Da mobilized troops behind him as support. It was then midwinter, and bitterly cold. For days crimson clouds had massed across the sky while the north wind roared wildly. When Song Jiang’s army arrived, Suo Chao went straight to Flying Tiger Ravine and made camp. The next day he led out his troops to meet the enemy. Song Jiang took Lü Fang and Guo Sheng of the forward division up a high hill to watch Guan Sheng fight. After three rolls of the battle drums, Guan Sheng rode out into the field. Suo Chao rode out from the opposing lines. When he saw Guan Sheng, he did not recognize him. A soldier accompanying him said, “The man approaching is Guan Sheng of the Great Blade, who has newly turned traitor.” On hearing this, Suo Chao said not a word but charged straight at Guan Sheng. Guan Sheng likewise spurred his horse forward, brandishing his blade to meet him. Before the two had fought ten bouts, Li Cheng, watching from the center, saw that Suo Chao’s axe was faltering and that he could not overcome Guan Sheng. Brandishing his twin swords, he rode out to attack Guan Sheng from the other side. Seeing this, Xuan Zan and Hao Siwen each took up his weapon and came forward to assist. The five horsemen became entangled in a single mêlée. Watching from the high ground, Song Jiang pointed with the tip of his whip. His whole army swept forward in a killing charge. Li Cheng’s forces suffered a crushing defeat and were hacked into scattered fragments; that very night they withdrew into the city and barred the gates, refusing to emerge. Song Jiang pressed his forces straight to the foot of the city walls and established camp. The next day, Suo Chao personally led a force out of the city in a sally. When Wu Yong saw this, he ordered his officers and soldiers to engage the enemy only in a feigned battle: “If he pursues, seize the moment and retreat.” Having won this engagement as well, Suo Chao returned happily to the city.

Then Suo Chao declared, “Last time I was struck by the bandits’ treacherous arrow. This time I shall avenge that injury.”
Counselor Liang immediately rewarded Suo Chao and ordered him to lead his own troops out of the city to meet the enemy.
Li Cheng and Wen Da mobilized troops behind him as support.
It was then midwinter, and bitterly cold. For days crimson clouds had massed across the sky while the north wind roared wildly.
When Song Jiang’s army arrived, Suo Chao went straight to Flying Tiger Ravine and made camp. The next day he led out his troops to meet the enemy.
Song Jiang took Lü Fang and Guo Sheng of the forward division up a high hill to watch Guan Sheng fight.
After three rolls of the battle drums, Guan Sheng rode out into the field.
Suo Chao rode out from the opposing lines. When he saw Guan Sheng, he did not recognize him.
A soldier accompanying him said, “The man approaching is Guan Sheng of the Great Blade, who has newly turned traitor.”
On hearing this, Suo Chao said not a word but charged straight at Guan Sheng.
Guan Sheng likewise spurred his horse forward, brandishing his blade to meet him.

Before the two had fought ten bouts, Li Cheng, watching from the center, saw that Suo Chao’s axe was faltering and that he could not overcome Guan Sheng. Brandishing his twin swords, he rode out to attack Guan Sheng from the other side.
Seeing this, Xuan Zan and Hao Siwen each took up his weapon and came forward to assist. The five horsemen became entangled in a single mêlée.

Watching from the high ground, Song Jiang pointed with the tip of his whip. His whole army swept forward in a killing charge. Li Cheng’s forces suffered a crushing defeat and were hacked into scattered fragments; that very night they withdrew into the city and barred the gates, refusing to emerge.
Song Jiang pressed his forces straight to the foot of the city walls and established camp.
The next day, Suo Chao personally led a force out of the city in a sally.
When Wu Yong saw this, he ordered his officers and soldiers to engage the enemy only in a feigned battle: “If he pursues, seize the moment and retreat.”
Having won this engagement as well, Suo Chao returned happily to the city.

p.src: That evening crimson clouds closed in from every side, and snow began to fall thick and fast. Wu Yong had already devised a plan. He secretly dispatched infantry to a narrow stretch of road beside the river at the foot of the hills outside Beijing, where they dug a pitfall and covered it with earth. That night the snow fell hard and the wind blew fiercely. At dawn, they saw that the snow lay about two feet deep. From the city walls they could see Song Jiang’s troops, all showing signs of fear and wavering restlessly between the eastern and western stockades. Suo Chao saw this, mustered three hundred mounted soldiers, and at once rode out of the city in pursuit. Song Jiang’s forces scattered and fled in every direction. But the naval chiefs Li Jun and Zhang Shun, clad in light armor, reined their horses across the way and leveled their spears as they came forward to meet the enemy. No sooner had they crossed weapons with Suo Chao than they cast down their spears and fled, deliberately drawing him toward the pitfall. Suo Chao was hot-tempered and paid no heed to his surroundings. There was a road on one side and a ravine on the other. Li Jun abandoned his horse and leapt into the ravine. Facing ahead, he cried out, “Brother Song Gongming, hurry and flee!” Hearing this, Suo Chao threw all caution for his own safety aside and galloped headlong through the formation. A cannon boomed behind the hill, and Suo Chao, horse and all, plunged into the pit.

p.src: The ambushers behind him rose as one. Even if Suo Chao had possessed three heads and six arms, he could not have escaped being battered and badly wounded. Deep beneath a covering of gleaming silver lay the snare; under a level carpet of shattered jade waited the pitfall. As for whether Suo Chao the Impatient Vanguard lived or died, listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
